@@ -0,0 +1,56 @@
+# Plan: Active-subspace reparameterization of rainfall-runoff calibration
+
+## Option being planned
+
+"Reparameterize the calibration with active subspaces to shorten the MCMC chain" — identify the few data-informed directions along which the negative log-likelihood varies (the active subspace), run Metropolis-Hastings only on those, and draw the inactive directions independently from the prior [s1]. The question this plan answers: **does the four-parameter GR4J calibration posterior admit a low-dimensional active subspace, and does running MCMC only on it beat both a serial chain and side-by-side chains — and is that verdict itself changed by buying more parallel compute?**
+
+## What to build
+
+1. **Differentiable GR4J forward model in JAX.** GR4J has exactly four calibrated parameters — production-store capacity X1 (mm), groundwater exchange X2 (mm/day), routing-store capacity X3 (mm), unit-hydrograph time base X4 (days) [s10]. Implement the webGR equations (production store, percolation, two unit hydrographs, routing store, groundwater exchange) so that the negative log-likelihood is differentiable w.r.t. all four parameters by automatic differentiation. This gives one forward **plus one adjoint pass** per gradient sample (or two forward evaluations by finite difference) [s7].
+2. **Active-subspace estimator.** Draw M independent prior samples; for each compute the misfit gradient ∇f; average the outer products into the matrix Ĉ = (1/M) Σ ∇fᵢ∇fᵢᵀ; eigendecompose. Report the eigenvalue spectrum λ1..λ4 and the spectral gap. This is the standard Monte Carlo estimator [s8].
+3. **Active-subspace MCMC.** Metropolis-Hastings on the n active variables (n = 1 or 2, chosen by the eigenvalue gap), with the per-step approximate likelihood ĝ(y) = (1/Mg) Σ f(W1·y + W2·zᵢ) using Mg = 10 conditional-average samples, and P = 10 independent prior draws on the inactive variables per reconstructed parameter [s1, s14]. Reconstruct the 4-D chain x = W1·y + W2·z.
+4. **Two baselines.** (a) *serial*: JAX-compiled random-walk Metropolis on all four parameters, proposal variance tuned to ~25% acceptance, 500,000 forward evaluations (the same budget the published comparison used) [s4]. (b) *copies*: independent vanilla chains started from dispersed points, one per GPU, run side by side.
+5. **Metric.** Minimum effective sample size (ESS) per component via the autocorrelation sum N/(1+2Σρₖ), exactly the published definition [s5], reported per forward evaluation and per wall-clock hour.
+
+## Baseline
+
+Vanilla random-walk Metropolis on all four GR4J parameters at 500,000 forward evaluations. In the published 100-parameter analogue this baseline reaches a minimum ESS of 604 while the active-subspace-accelerated chain reaches 81,986 at the same evaluation budget [s5]. The GR4J comparison reuses the identical budget and definition; the only differences are the 4-parameter forward model and the artificial bimodality that cheap fixed-step integration is known to inject [s9].
+
+## How to check it is right
+
+1. **Anchor — reproduce the published two-parameter quadratic.** Forward model m(x) = ½·xᵀAx with A = Q·diag(1, ε)·Qᵀ, Q = ½[[√2,√2],[−√2,√2]], noise σ² = 0.1, data d = 0.9 [s1]. With ε = 0.01 the paper reports "the gap between the eigenvalues suggests an active one-dimensional active subspace" [s6]; with ε = 0.95 there is no gap. My estimator must recover λ1/λ2 ≳ 100 at ε = 0.01 and λ1/λ2 ≲ 10 at ε = 0.95, matching the published scripts (bitbucket.org/paulcon/accelerating-mcmc-with-active-subspaces). Failing this stops the spend.
+2. **Forward-model check.** The JAX GR4J must reproduce the webGR equations verbatim and match the airGR reference on a fixed parameter set.
+3. **ESS magnitude check.** The accelerated chain's min-ESS jump must reproduce the published 604 → 81,986 magnitude [s5] before I trust the GR4J result.
+4. **Bias check.** The accelerated chain's posterior mean and covariance must match a long serial reference chain within a stated tolerance (the Hellinger-distance bound the paper derives [s1]).
+
+## The compute question (what the money actually tests)
+
+The pipeline is four serial steps: draw M gradient samples → average outer products → eigendecompose → run the active-variable chain. The M gradient samples are mutually independent, so they run concurrently across GPUs; only the eigendecomposition and the short low-dimensional chain stay serial. The quantity more parallel compute buys is therefore **M, the number of gradient samples**. The published demos stop at M = 300 (one-dimensional subspace) [s8] and M = 1000 (100-parameter model, two-dimensional subspace) [s3]. The plan sweeps M ∈ {100, 300, 1000, 10000, 100000} on GR4J and asks whether the eigenvalue gap and the accelerated-chain ESS verdict change with M:
+
+- **if_lever**: more samples make the gap appear/widen, so the accelerated chain only beats both baselines at high M.
+- **if_not**: the gap is already clear at M = 300, so 100× more samples change nothing — compute is not the lever, the reparameterization is.
+
+Decision rule: compute is the lever only if λ1/λ2 at 100,000 samples is ≥ 2× that at 300, or the accelerated chain's min-ESS at 100,000 is ≥ 2× that at 300; otherwise compute is not the lever. Noise rule: 10 independent prior-sample batches for bootstrap spectral ranges, 3 seeds per MCMC run, differences declared only on non-overlapping ranges.
+
+## Cost
+
+Rates (Lambda on-demand, read 2026-10-20): 1× NVIDIA A6000 (48 GB) at $1.09/GPU/hr [s12]; 8× NVIDIA A100 SXM (80 GB) at $2.79/GPU/hr [s13]. Filesystem ~$0.20/GiB-month.
+
+| line | phase | instance | hours | cost |
+|---|---|---|---|---|
+| pilot: JAX GR4J + 1000-sample spectral estimate, time it | pilot | 1×A6000 | 2 h (need ≈ 0.5 h) | $2.18 |
+| reproduce: two-parameter anchor + ESS comparison | reproduce | 1×A6000 | 2 h (need ≈ 0.5 h) | $2.18 |
+| spectrum sweep M∈{100…100000} | spectrum_sweep | 1×A6000 | 2 h (need ≈ 0.2 h) | $2.18 |
+| three arms at 500k evaluations | mcmc_compare | 1×A6000 | 4 h (need ≈ 1 h) | $4.36 |
+| optional: 671-catchment CAMELS sweep | camels | 8×A100 | 2 h (need ≈ 0.6 h) | $44.64 |
+| storage (CAMELS forcing + results, 5 GiB) | camels | — | — | $1.00 |
+
+**Total ≈ $56.54, hard stop $200.** The fact that this sits ~$57 under the $1000 ceiling is itself the answer to the root question: for a four-parameter lumped model the active-subspace computation is not compute-bound. The only line that meaningfully uses parallel GPUs is the 671-catchment sweep, and even that is minutes of GPU time.
+
+## What $1000 cannot buy here
+
+The genuinely compute-bound extension — active-subspace reparameterization of a hundreds-of-parameter distributed model (the high-performance-computing regime the framer names) across all catchments — is out of scope at any price near this budget and is left open.
+
+## Human time / outside budget
+
+~8 hours of my time writing and debugging the JAX pipeline; CAMELS download (a few GiB, free).

1: # What actually limits Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models — and whether "a shit ton of GPUs" fixes it
2: 
3: ## 1. My understanding, relayed before answering
4: 
5: Rainfall-runoff (RR) models map precipitation (and potential evapotranspiration) onto streamflow at a catchment outlet. The workhorse class for calibration studies is the lumped conceptual model — GR4J is the canonical example, with exactly **four** calibrated parameters and a simple production-store + unit-hydrograph structure evaluated a few thousand arithmetic steps per decade of daily data (Perrin, Michel & Andréassian 2003, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257). Bayesian calibration treats parameters as random and uses Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample the posterior p(θ | data).
6: 
7: Two facts dominate this literature:
8: 
9: 1. **Equifinality** — many different parameter sets reproduce the observed hydrograph almost equally well, so the posterior is broad, correlated, and often multimodal rather than a tight Gaussian around a single optimum. Beven & Binley (1992) state it directly: "within the limitations of a given model structure and errors in boundary conditions and field observations, different sets of values may be equally likely as simulators of a catchment" (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305).
10: 2. **Peculiar response surfaces** — hydrological model parameters are "highly correlated and interdependent," which is precisely what makes naive samplers mix slowly; summarizing/exploring the posterior is the stated bottleneck that "hindered widespread use of Bayesian techniques in hydrology" (Marshall, Nott & Sharma 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378). MCMC inefficiency is "frequently caused by an inappropriate selection of the proposal distribution" — a geometric/algorithmic problem, not a hardware one (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).
11: 
12: MCMC samples are autocorrelated. The information content of a chain of length N is the effective sample size ESS = N / (1 + 2Σρ_k), where ρ_k are lag autocorrelations; slow mixing inflates the integrated autocorrelation time τ and forces long chains to reach any target ESS (Stan Reference Manual, https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html). The integrated autocorrelation time is defined as the number of correlated samples needed, on average, to produce one independent draw (LaplacesDemon IAT/ESS documentation, https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/LaplacesDemon/help/ESS.html). So "needs long MCMC chains" is a symptom of large τ — a statistical property — not directly a statement about hardware speed.
13: 
14: ## 2. Predictions (stated before checking)
15: 
16: - **P1:** For a single lumped conceptual catchment, one forward run is so cheap that the likelihood is effectively free; the binding constraint is τ (mixing), not FLOPs.
17: - **P2:** The "long chains" requirement is a property of posterior geometry (correlation/equifinality/multimodality) and, secondarily, of numerical implementation; it is reduced by better samplers/reparameterizations, not by more cores.
18: - **P3:** GPUs help only where the problem decomposes into independent units of work: many chains (ensemble MCMC), many particles (SMC), many catchments (large-sample), or many forward runs (GLUE / expensive models). They cannot shorten a *single* chain's autocorrelation.
19: - **P4:** There are genuinely compute-bound levels — expensive distributed/high-dimensional models and large-sample (CAMELS-scale) studies — where more parallel compute changes what is even attempted.
20: 
21: ## 3. Analysis
22: 
23: ### 3.1 Why chains are long: geometry and numerics, not throughput
24:

# What actually limits Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models — and whether "a shit ton of GPUs" fixes it

## 1. My understanding, relayed before answering

Rainfall-runoff (RR) models map precipitation (and potential evapotranspiration) onto streamflow at a catchment outlet. The workhorse class for calibration studies is the lumped conceptual model — GR4J is the canonical example, with exactly **four** calibrated parameters and a simple production-store + unit-hydrograph structure evaluated a few thousand arithmetic steps per decade of daily data (Perrin, Michel & Andréassian 2003, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257). Bayesian calibration treats parameters as random and uses Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample the posterior p(θ | data).

Two facts dominate this literature:

1. **Equifinality** — many different parameter sets reproduce the observed hydrograph almost equally well, so the posterior is broad, correlated, and often multimodal rather than a tight Gaussian around a single optimum. Beven & Binley (1992) state it directly: "within the limitations of a given model structure and errors in boundary conditions and field observations, different sets of values may be equally likely as simulators of a catchment" (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305).
2. **Peculiar response surfaces** — hydrological model parameters are "highly correlated and interdependent," which is precisely what makes naive samplers mix slowly; summarizing/exploring the posterior is the stated bottleneck that "hindered widespread use of Bayesian techniques in hydrology" (Marshall, Nott & Sharma 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378). MCMC inefficiency is "frequently caused by an inappropriate selection of the proposal distribution" — a geometric/algorithmic problem, not a hardware one (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).

MCMC samples are autocorrelated. The information content of a chain of length N is the effective sample size ESS = N / (1 + 2Σρ_k), where ρ_k are lag autocorrelations; slow mixing inflates the integrated autocorrelation time τ and forces long chains to reach any target ESS (Stan Reference Manual, https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html). The integrated autocorrelation time is defined as the number of correlated samples needed, on average, to produce one independent draw (LaplacesDemon IAT/ESS documentation, https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/LaplacesDemon/help/ESS.html). So "needs long MCMC chains" is a symptom of large τ — a statistical property — not directly a statement about hardware speed.

## 2. Predictions (stated before checking)

- **P1:** For a single lumped conceptual catchment, one forward run is so cheap that the likelihood is effectively free; the binding constraint is τ (mixing), not FLOPs.
- **P2:** The "long chains" requirement is a property of posterior geometry (correlation/equifinality/multimodality) and, secondarily, of numerical implementation; it is reduced by better samplers/reparameterizations, not by more cores.
- **P3:** GPUs help only where the problem decomposes into independent units of work: many chains (ensemble MCMC), many particles (SMC), many catchments (large-sample), or many forward runs (GLUE / expensive models). They cannot shorten a *single* chain's autocorrelation.
- **P4:** There are genuinely compute-bound levels — expensive distributed/high-dimensional models and large-sample (CAMELS-scale) studies — where more parallel compute changes what is even attempted.

Modern physics and engineering simulations take several inputs—e.g., boundary conditions, material properties, and forcings—and output several quantities of interests. When the gradient is not available as a black box, one might estimate the gradient through evaluations of ff, e.g., with finite differences or related techniques \[[20](#bib.bib20)\]. A first-order finite difference approximation to the gradient vector requires m+1m+1 evaluations of ff, so estimating 𝑪^\\widehat{\\bm{C}} in ([4](#S1.E4 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) takes M⁡(m+1)M(m+1) evaluations, which may be prohibitively expensive for large-scale simulations. ## IV Conclusion

We have studied the approximation properties of two methods for estimating the eigenvectors and eigenvalues that define a multivariate function’s active subspace. These methods use linear measurements of the gradient instead of the full gradient, which can be efficiently computed with finite differences. The first method, based on work by Qi and Hughes \[[21](#bib.bib21)\], uses random projections of the gradient. The second uses a low-rank approximation of the matrix of gradient measurements fit with an alternating least-squares method. The low-rank approximation performs better than the projection-based method in two numerical tests. Future work will (i) analyze the improvement with the low-rank approximation and (ii) study the effect of finite difference approximations of the linear measurements. These initial results are sufficiently promising to pursue such studies.

###### Abstract
The Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method is the computational workhorse for Bayesian inverse problems. However, MCMC struggles in high-dimensional parameter spaces, since its iterates must sequentially explore the high-dimensional space. This struggle is compounded in physical applications when the nonlinear forward model is computationally expensive. One approach to accelerate MCMC is to reduce the dimension of the state space. *Active subspaces* are part of an emerging set of tools for subspace-based dimension reduction. An active subspace in a given inverse problem indicates a separation between a low-dimensional subspace that is informed by the data and its orthogonal complement that is constrained by the prior. With this information, one can run the sequential MCMC on the active variables while sampling independently according to the prior on the inactive variables. However, this approach to increase efficiency may introduce bias. We provide a bound on the Hellinger distance between the true posterior and its active subspace-exploiting approximation. And we demonstrate the active subspace-accelerated MCMC on two computational examples: (i) a two-dimensional parameter space with a quadratic forward model and one-dimensional active subspace and (ii) a 100-dimensional parameter space with a PDE-based forward model and a two-dimensional active subspace.

## 1 Introduction
Modern computing enables powerful Bayesian inference methods to quantify uncertainty in complex science and engineering models. The workhorse of these methods is Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which constructs a Markov chain whose steps produce correlated samples from the conditional posterior density of the parameters given data. Several excellent references introduce and develop the theory and practice of MCMC in the context of statistical inverse problems [3, 22, 27]. However, standard MCMC remains an inefficient tool when (i) the dimension of the parameter space is large and/or (ii) the forward model in the likelihood is expensive. Recent papers have proposed strategies to increase MCMC’s efficiency by introducing structure-exploiting proposal densities [1, 20, 28, 18, 24, 5]. When the forward model numerically approximates a PDE solution, the differential operators may enable MCMC variants whose state space dimension is independent of the PDE discretization [4, 5, 24, 14].
MCMC struggles in high dimensions because the Markov chain must explore the high-dimensional space to find regions of relatively high posterior probability. The recent paper by Cui, et al. [14] seeks to reduce the Markov chain’s state space dimension by identifying a low-dimensional *likelihood-informed subspace*. When an inverse problem is ill-posed, the data does not inform all parameters; Cui, et al. use the eigendecomposition of the negative log-likelihood’s Hessian—averaged over the parameter space with respect to the posterior—to identify a data-informed subspace; its orthogonal complement is informed by the prior. This separation leads to an efficient MCMC method when the forward model is twice differentiable, the prior is Gaussian, and the noise is Gaussian. They have extended these ideas to develop optimal posterior covariance approximations for linear forward models [26] and dimension-independent methods for infinite dimensional problems [13].
Our recent work in *active subspaces* resembles the subspace-based dimension reduction of Cui, et al. [14], though the context is broader than statistical inverse problems. The active subspace is defined for a scalar-valued, multivariate function; the active subspace basis consists of the principal eigenvectors of the average outer product of the gradient with itself. When a function admits an active subspace, one can exploit the low-dimensional structure to enable approximation, integration, and optimization in high dimensions [9, 11, 8]. We have applied this technique to help study aerospace models [10, 23], hydrological models [21], and solar cell models [12]. We review active subspaces and the resulting approximations in section 2.
In this paper, we seek to discover the active subspace from the negative log-likelihood in a Bayesian inverse problem. If the negative log-likelihood admits an active subspace, then we use the active subspace to construct a function that approximates the Bayesian posterior. The approximate posterior enables an efficient MCMC that exploits the low-dimensional structure; the Markov chain operates on the active variables (i.e., the coordinates of the active subspace), while the inactive variables are drawn independently from their derived prior. In contrast to the likelihood-informed subspace of Cui, et al. [14], the active subspace is defined by the gradient of the negative log-likelihood instead of a Gauss-Newton-based approximation of its Hessian. Additionally, the matrix that defines the active subspace is an average with respect to the prior as opposed to the posterior. This choice is computationally appealing, since one can draw independent samples from the prior and estimate integrals with standard Monte Carlo. Consequently, computing the active subspace is a preprocessing step that occurs before the MCMC.
In section 3, we analyze the approximation error in the posterior, measured by the Hellinger distance. We detail the MCMC algorithm with the active subspace in section 4. We demonstrate the approach in two synthetic Bayesian inverse problems: (i) a quadratic forward model with a two-dimensional parameter space and (ii) a forward model governed by Poisson’s equation, where the data are the PDE solution—perturbed by noise—at points on the boundary, and the parameters are the coefficients of the differential operator. We describe the models and show results in section 5. In section 6, we summarize the method and discuss some practical limitations and future work.
